summary: Describes SOCKS version 5, a protocol that lets a client connect through a firewall or proxy server. It supports pluggable authentication and is an evolution of version 4. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: SOCKS is a protocol that lets a program reach the outside world through a proxy server that sits behind a firewall. The program says who it is, asks the server to make the connection, and gets an answer saying whether the request was allowed.

subtitle: A general framework that lets TCP and UDP applications pass through a firewall via a SOCKS server, with pluggable authentication.

tldr.problem: Firewalls isolate an internal network, and applications need a general, authenticated way to traverse them rather than relying on per-protocol gateways.
tldr.mechanism: The client opens a TCP connection to the SOCKS server, negotiates an authentication method, then sends a CONNECT, BIND or UDP ASSOCIATE request and gets back a reply with a bound address and port.
tldr.outcome: Version 5 extends SOCKS version 4 with UDP support, strong authentication methods and domain-name and IPv6 addressing.

today: RFC 1928 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text defers the method-specific sub-negotiations to separate memos.

sections.title: Why SOCKS Exists
sections.content:
Network firewalls, systems that effectively isolate an organization's internal network structure from an exterior network such as the Internet, are becoming increasingly popular. These firewall systems typically act as application-layer gateways between networks, usually offering controlled TELNET, FTP and SMTP access. With the emergence of more sophisticated application-layer protocols designed to facilitate global information discovery, there is a need for a general framework for these protocols to traverse a firewall transparently and securely.

There is also a need for strong authentication of such traversal in as fine-grained a manner as is practical. This stems from the realization that client-server relationships emerge between the networks of various organizations, and that such relationships need to be controlled and often strongly authenticated.

The protocol is designed to provide a framework for client-server applications in both the TCP and UDP domains to conveniently and securely use the services of a network firewall. It is conceptually a shim layer between the application layer and the transport layer, so it does not provide network-layer gateway services such as forwarding ICMP messages.

SOCKS version 4 already provides unsecured firewall traversal for TCP-based client-server applications, including TELNET, FTP and the information-discovery protocols HTTP, WAIS and GOPHER. Version 5 extends that model to include UDP, extends the framework to include provisions for generalized strong authentication schemes, and extends the addressing scheme to encompass domain names and IPv6 addresses. Implementing SOCKS typically involves recompiling or relinking TCP-based client applications to use the appropriate encapsulation routines in the SOCKS library.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall separates an organization’s machines from the rest of the Internet. SOCKS gives applications one way past it, with a check on identity that is finer grained than the per-protocol gateways firewalls usually offer.

sections.title: Connecting and Choosing Authentication
sections.content:
When a TCP-based client wishes to reach an object reachable only via a firewall, and the determination of that is left up to the implementation, it must open a TCP connection to the SOCKS port on the SOCKS server system. The SOCKS service is conventionally located on TCP port 1080. If the request succeeds, the client enters a negotiation for the authentication method to be used, authenticates with the chosen method, then sends a relay request. The server evaluates the request and either establishes the appropriate connection or denies it.

The client sends a version identifier and method selection message with three fields. VER is one octet and is set to X'05'. NMETHODS is one octet and holds the number of method identifier octets that follow. METHODS is 1 to 255 octets.

The server selects from one of the methods given and replies with a METHOD selection message, which is a VER octet and a METHOD octet. If the selected method is X'FF', none of the methods listed by the client is acceptable, and the client MUST close the connection. The defined method values are X'00' for no authentication required, X'01' for GSSAPI, X'02' for username and password, X'03' to X'7F' for IANA assigned methods, X'80' to X'FE' reserved for private methods, and X'FF' for no acceptable methods.

The client and server then enter a method-specific sub-negotiation, whose descriptions appear in separate memos. Developers of new METHOD support should contact IANA for a METHOD number. Compliant implementations MUST support GSSAPI and SHOULD support username and password authentication methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The client opens a connection to the SOCKS server and lists the ways it can prove who it is. The server picks one of them, or answers with a value meaning none of them will do, and the client then closes the connection.

sections.title: The Request and How Addresses Are Given
sections.content:
Once the method-dependent sub-negotiation has completed, the client sends the request details. If the negotiated method includes encapsulation for integrity checking or confidentiality, these requests MUST be encapsulated in the method-dependent encapsulation.

The request has six fields. VER is the protocol version, X'05'. CMD is the command. RSV is reserved and must be set to X'00'. ATYP is the address type of the following address. DST.ADDR is the desired destination address, of variable length. DST.PORT is the desired destination port in network octet order, two octets.

The ATYP field says what kind of address follows. X'01' is a version-4 IP address of 4 octets. X'03' is a fully-qualified domain name, where the first octet of the address field contains the number of octets of name that follow and there is no terminating NUL octet. X'04' is a version-6 IP address of 16 octets. The same three values apply to the ATYP field of the reply.

The server typically evaluates the request based on source and destination addresses, and returns one or more reply messages as appropriate for the request type. The reply has the same shape: VER, a REP reply field, reserved RSV, ATYP, BND.ADDR and BND.PORT. The reply field values are X'00' succeeded, X'01' general SOCKS server failure, X'02' connection not allowed by ruleset, X'03' network unreachable, X'04' host unreachable, X'05' connection refused, X'06' TTL expired, X'07' command not supported, X'08' address type not supported, and X'09' to X'FF' unassigned. If the chosen method includes encapsulation for authentication, integrity or confidentiality, the replies are encapsulated in the method-dependent encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The client then sends a request naming the command and the destination, and the server replies with a status code plus the address and port it assigned. The destination can be given as an IP address or as a domain name.

sections.title: The Three Commands
sections.content:
There are three commands. CONNECT, X'01', asks the server to connect to the destination. In the reply to a CONNECT, BND.PORT contains the port number the server assigned to connect to the target host and BND.ADDR the associated IP address. The supplied BND.ADDR is often different from the IP address the client uses to reach the SOCKS server, since such servers are often multi-homed. The server is expected to use DST.ADDR and DST.PORT, and the client-side source address and port, when evaluating the request.

BIND, X'02', is for protocols where the client must accept a connection from the server. FTP is the well-known example, using the primary client-to-server connection for commands and status reports but a server-to-client connection for transferring data on demand. The client side of an application protocol is expected to use BIND only to establish secondary connections after a primary connection has been established using CONNECT. Two replies are sent during a BIND operation. The first is sent after the server creates and binds a new socket, and BND.PORT holds the port number the server assigned to listen for an incoming connection while BND.ADDR holds the associated IP address. The client will typically use these to notify the application server of the rendezvous address, over the primary or control connection. The second reply occurs only after the anticipated incoming connection succeeds or fails, and its BND.PORT and BND.ADDR hold the address and port number of the connecting host.

UDP ASSOCIATE, X'03', establishes an association within the UDP relay process to handle UDP datagrams. Its DST.ADDR and DST.PORT hold the address and port the client expects to use to send UDP datagrams on for the association, and the server MAY use this information to limit access to the association. If the client does not have that information at the time of the request, it MUST use a port number and address of all zeros. A UDP association terminates when the TCP connection that the UDP ASSOCIATE request arrived on terminates. In the reply, BND.PORT and BND.ADDR indicate the port number and address where the client MUST send UDP request messages to be relayed.

When a reply with a failure code indicates a failure, the server MUST terminate the TCP connection shortly after sending the reply, and no more than 10 seconds after detecting the condition that caused the failure. If the reply indicates success and the request was either a BIND or a CONNECT, the client may now start passing data, encapsulated using the method-dependent encapsulation if the selected authentication method supports it. When data arrives at the server for the client, the server MUST encapsulate it as appropriate for the method in use.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three commands: make the connection, wait for someone to make a connection to you, or set up a mailbox for datagrams. A failure reply names the reason, and the server closes the connection within ten seconds.

sections.title: Relaying UDP Datagrams
sections.content:
A UDP-based client MUST send its datagrams to the UDP relay server at the UDP port indicated by BND.PORT in the reply to the UDP ASSOCIATE request. If the selected authentication method provides encapsulation for authenticity, integrity or confidentiality, the datagram MUST be encapsulated using the appropriate encapsulation.

Each UDP datagram carries a UDP request header with it. RSV is a two-octet reserved field set to X'0000'. FRAG is one octet giving the current fragment number. ATYP is one octet naming the address type, with the same three values as in the request. DST.ADDR is the desired destination address, of variable length. DST.PORT is the desired destination port, two octets. DATA is the user data, of variable length.

When the UDP relay server decides to relay a datagram, it does so silently, without notifying the requesting client, and it drops datagrams it cannot or will not relay. When it receives a reply datagram from a remote host, it MUST encapsulate that datagram using the same UDP request header and any authentication-method-dependent encapsulation. The relay server MUST acquire from the SOCKS server the expected IP address of the client that will send datagrams to the BND.PORT given in the UDP ASSOCIATE reply, and it MUST drop any datagrams arriving from any source IP address other than the one recorded for that association.

The FRAG field indicates whether the datagram is one of a number of fragments. If implemented, the high-order bit indicates end-of-fragment sequence, a value of X'00' indicates a standalone datagram, and values between 1 and 127 indicate the fragment position within a sequence. Each receiver has a reassembly queue and a reassembly timer associated with these fragments. The queue must be reinitialized and the associated fragments abandoned whenever the timer expires, or a new datagram arrives carrying a FRAG value less than the highest FRAG value processed for that sequence. The reassembly timer MUST be no less than 5 seconds, and applications are advised to avoid fragmentation wherever possible. Implementation of fragmentation is optional; an implementation that does not support it MUST drop any datagram whose FRAG field is other than X'00'.

The programming interface for a SOCKS-aware UDP MUST report an available buffer space for UDP datagrams that is smaller than the actual space provided by the operating system: 10 plus method-dependent octets smaller when ATYP is X'01', 262 plus method-dependent octets smaller when it is X'03', and 20 plus method-dependent octets smaller when it is X'04'.
sections.plainLanguage: For the datagram mailbox, each datagram carries a small header naming its destination. The relay forwards them silently and drops any that arrive from an address other than the one it recorded for that mailbox.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document describes a protocol for the application-layer traversal of IP network firewalls. The security of such traversal is highly dependent on the particular authentication and encapsulation methods provided in a particular implementation, and selected during negotiation between the SOCKS client and the SOCKS server. Careful consideration should be given by the administrator to the selection of authentication methods.
sections.plainLanguage: How safe the traversal is depends on the authentication and encapsulation methods the implementation offers and the ones chosen during negotiation, so administrators should pick the method carefully.
